name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)
oneLiner: A structured talk therapy — the best-evidenced tinnitus treatment. It doesn't quiet the sound, but reliably reduces its impact on your life.
whatItIs: A structured, time-limited talking therapy (typically 8–12 sessions) that changes unhelpful thought patterns and behaviors around tinnitus, delivered by psychologists or trained clinicians, in person or online.
howItWorks: Tinnitus distress is driven largely by the brain's threat response to the sound — attention, arousal and negative appraisal keep it loud in awareness. CBT breaks that loop: the sound may not change, but the brain stops treating it as a threat, so it intrudes less.
mechanism: Cognitive restructuring + habituation of the threat response

loudness.summary: Cochrane: only weak, if any, effects on perceived loudness. CBT is not shown to make tinnitus quieter.

distress.summary: SMD −0.56 vs no treatment (≈11 THI points); beats audiological care and TRT; confirmed as a top single treatment by UNITI 2025.

regulatory.detail: Recommended by the AAO-HNSF clinical practice guideline (2014, update in development) and international guidelines.

availability.usa: Widely available via psychologists; access limited by therapist supply

safety: Essentially no reported harms in the Cochrane review (moderate certainty).
bestSuitedFor: Anyone with bothersome tinnitus, especially with anxiety, low mood or sleep disruption
bestResult: ≈11 THI-point advantage vs no treatment; up to 15.8 points vs TRT in one trial
limitations: Does not change loudness
Mostly low-certainty evidence with little long-term follow-up
Therapist availability limits access

timeline.event: First CBT protocols adapted for tinnitus distress.
AAO-HNSF guideline recommends CBT for persistent bothersome tinnitus.
Cochrane review: 28 studies, 2,733 participants — consistent quality-of-life benefit.
UNITI-RCT (N=461): CBT among the largest single-treatment effects; combinations add little.

latest.text: UNITI-RCT published in Nature Communications: CBT and hearing aids alone showed the largest effect sizes; combining treatments was compensatory, not synergistic.

history.reason: Largest controlled evidence base in the field; benefit limited to distress, hence not 5/5.

scoreRationale: 28 RCTs and consistent replication earn a 4/5 — held back from 5/5 because certainty is mostly low, follow-up is short, and the benefit is confined to distress, not the percept.

name: Auricle bisensory stimulation (Susan Shore device)
oneLiner: The only treatment with rigorous randomized evidence of making tinnitus quieter — still stuck in the lab.
whatItIs: A home-use device from Susan Shore's University of Michigan lab that pairs precisely timed sound (matched to your tinnitus spectrum) with mild electrical stimulation of the face or neck, 30 minutes a day. Licensed to Auricle Inc. Not for sale anywhere.
howItWorks: In somatic tinnitus, fusiform cells in the dorsal cochlear nucleus fire in pathological synchrony. Precisely timed auditory + somatosensory input exploits spike-timing-dependent plasticity to desynchronize them — targeting the root circuit rather than the reaction to it.
mechanism: Timing-dependent plasticity in the dorsal cochlear nucleus

loudness.summary: Loudness was a CO-PRIMARY endpoint, measured by psychoacoustic loudness matching (dB SL): within-participant change −7.2 dB per-protocol (p=.03) at week 6, deepening to −14.1 dB by week 12 of the second active phase — the strongest percept-level result of any tinnitus RCT. These are changes during treatment, not active-minus-control differences.

distress.summary: TFI (the other co-primary): −12.0 ITT / −13.2 per-protocol after active treatment, at the clinically meaningful threshold; the control block produced no clinically significant decrease. ≥13-point responders: 65% per-protocol / 53% ITT vs 25%/20% control.

regulatory.detail: No FDA authorization of any kind; only one device (Lenire) has ever been authorized in the bimodal tinnitus class (QVN). Claims of Breakthrough Device designation could not be verified. No trial sponsored by Auricle Inc is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov as of Sept 2026 (don't confuse it with 'Auricle Health Inc', an unrelated company running a hearing-restoration study, NCT07402941).

subtypes: somatic tinnitus (can modulate tinnitus with jaw/neck movements)
safety: No serious adverse events reported in trials; mild, well-tolerated stimulation.
bestSuitedFor: Somatic tinnitus with normal-to-moderate hearing loss — the only population studied
bestResult: 65% per-protocol TFI responders (vs 25% control) and loudness matching −14.1 dB (cumulative, per-protocol) in the 2023 crossover RCT
limitations: Single-center evidence; per-protocol n=56
Somatic tinnitus only
No registered pivotal trial, no FDA submission, and company silence since 2023 — commercial timeline unknown
conflicts: NIH funded the trials, but Shore and Martel cofounded Auricle and hold equity and patent interests (disclosed).

timeline.event: First-in-human pilot (N=20) in Science Translational Medicine.
Main crossover trial completes (NCT03621735).
JAMA Network Open publishes the N=99 double-blind crossover: loudness and TFI both improve.
Auricle declines to comment on timing; no pivotal trial registered.

latest.text: Third-party status check: still no FDA approval and no confirmed release date; Auricle remains silent on timing.

history.change: Phase 2 audit: ranking moved #2 → #3 (swapped with Lenire)
history.reason: Adversarial review judged #2 to be novelty bias: one single-center crossover trial, somatic subtype only, per-protocol n=56, no independent replication, no registered pivotal trial, no regulatory progress in three years. The within-trial rigor (double-blind, co-primary loudness endpoint) keeps it at #3.
Uniquely strong loudness evidence, but single-center, subtype-limited, and unreplicated.

scoreRationale: A rigorous NIH-funded double-blind crossover with percept-level benefit earns a 3/5; independent replication, a pivotal trial, and regulatory progress would raise it.
narrowNote: Studied ONLY in somatic tinnitus — people who can change their tinnitus by moving the jaw or neck — with normal-to-moderate hearing loss.

name: Lenire (bimodal tongue stimulation)
oneLiner: Pairs sound with mild tongue stimulation — the first and only device of its type the FDA has authorized for tinnitus. Large trials and real-world data, but all company-funded and none with a placebo group.
whatItIs: A prescription device from Neuromod (Dublin): headphones deliver sound while a small mouthpiece ('Tonguetip') delivers mild electrical pulses to the tongue, typically 30–60 minutes daily for 12 weeks, fitted at trained clinics.
howItWorks: Pairing auditory input with trigeminal (tongue) stimulation is intended to drive plasticity in auditory brain circuits and reduce the network activity underlying tinnitus — the same bimodal principle as the Shore device, via a different somatosensory channel.
mechanism: Bimodal auditory + trigeminal stimulation driving auditory-circuit plasticity

loudness.summary: No published psychoacoustic loudness-matching benefit. All primary endpoints are THI (a distress/handicap instrument).

distress.summary: Consistent within-arm THI improvements across TENT-A1/A2/A3 and real-world cohorts — but no trial had a sham arm, the pivotal trial's full-cohort primary endpoint was missed, and the pre-specified benefit appeared only in the moderate-or-worse (THI≥38) subgroup.

regulatory.detail: De Novo DEN210033 granted March 6, 2023 — the only device in FDA's bimodal tinnitus-treatment classification (21 CFR 874.3410, product code QVN). Precision matters: dozens of tinnitus MASKERS (Neuromonics, Levo, Widex Zen, SilentCloud…) hold 510(k) clearances under the separate masker regulation 874.3400, so 'only FDA-authorized tinnitus device' would be wrong. This is also not a PMA 'approval' — company marketing that says 'FDA approved' overstates the pathway. Also CE-marked in Europe.

availability.usa: Available by prescription through trained audiology/ENT clinics; available to veterans through the VA
availability.cost: ≈$3,200–4,750 self-pay (commonly ~$4,000) including fitting and follow-up; generally not insurance-covered

subtypes: chronic subjective tinnitus, moderate or worse severity (best-supported group)
safety: 96.8% of device-related adverse events in the pivotal trial were mild; no serious device-related events.
bestSuitedFor: Moderate-to-severe tinnitus (THI ≥ 38) — the subgroup where bimodal beat sound-only
bestResult: TENT-A3 severe subgroup: 58.6% vs 43.2% responders (p=0.022); TENT-A2 within-arm THI −18.5 at end of treatment; real-world mean THI −23.8 at 12 weeks (uncontrolled, 66/104 analyzed)
limitations: No trial has ever included a sham/no-treatment arm — within-arm improvements can't be separated from placebo/natural course
TENT-A3's full-cohort primary endpoint was NOT achieved; the authorization rests on the severe subgroup
Every study is manufacturer-funded or manufacturer-linked
Expensive and rarely covered by insurance
conflicts: All trials funded by Neuromod; key author Hubert Lim is Neuromod's CSO with a financial interest.

timeline.event: TENT-A1 begins in Ireland.
TENT-A1 published in Science Translational Medicine (N=326).
TENT-A2 published (N=191).
FDA De Novo authorization (March 6); US launch via clinics and the VA.
TENT-A3 pivotal published in Nature Communications — subgroup benefit only.
Second US real-world chart review published (AJA).

latest.text: Real-world US chart review (N=140): 81.8% of bothered-tinnitus patients improved ≥7 THI points, mean −23.8 — retrospective and manufacturer-linked, so placebo/natural course can't be excluded.

history.change: Phase 2 audit: ranking moved #3 → #2 (swapped with the Shore/Auricle device)
history.reason: Replication across three trials and two real-world cohorts, regulatory authorization, and actual availability outweigh a single unreplicated crossover trial — ranking an unavailable device above an authorized one was novelty bias. Caveats unchanged: no sham arm anywhere, all evidence manufacturer-funded.
Large trials and FDA De Novo authorization, offset by absent placebo controls and universal manufacturer funding.

scoreRationale: Three large trials, regulatory authorization and real-world consistency earn 3/5 — capped there because no sham-controlled arm exists, the pivotal full-cohort endpoint was missed (severe-subgroup benefit only), and there is no independent replication.

name: Digital CBT & app-based therapeutics
oneLiner: CBT's evidence, delivered by app — the fastest-maturing corner of the field, with the first sham-controlled wins.
whatItIs: Smartphone-delivered structured tinnitus programs — CBT-based courses, sound tools and guided coaching. Examples with real trial evidence: Kalmeda (Germany, prescribable DiGA), Oto (UK), SilentCloud (CE-marked, FDA 510(k)-cleared), MindEar, and audiologist-guided iCBT platforms.
howItWorks: Same mechanism as CBT — reframing the brain's response to the sound — plus scale: an app can reach people who will never see a tinnitus-trained psychologist.
mechanism: CBT techniques delivered digitally, sometimes with sound therapy and clinician support

loudness.summary: All app RCT primary outcomes are distress instruments (TFI/THI/TQ); none demonstrates loudness reduction.

distress.summary: Kalmeda RCT N=187: d=1.1 (vs delayed treatment — inflates vs sham designs). Japan 2026 double-blind sham-app RCT: THI −20.4 between groups at week 16. Oto RCT: between-group 16 TFI points at 6 months (unblinded, waitlist). iCBT: d=0.46.

regulatory.detail: Kalmeda: permanently listed in Germany's DiGA registry (#350, permanent since Dec 2021 — prescribable, reimbursed). SilentCloud: FDA 510(k) K221125 (Jan 2023) — cleared as a tinnitus MASKER ('relief... while using the device', fitted by a hearing professional), plus EU MDR CE mark per the manufacturer. Most other apps are unregulated wellness products — check each one.

availability.usa: App stores; SilentCloud cleared; most others wellness-tier
availability.europe: Kalmeda prescribable in Germany; others via app stores
availability.cost: Free–$30/month typical; Kalmeda reimbursed in Germany

developer: Multiple (mynoise GmbH/Kalmeda, Oto Health, SilentCloud, MindEar…)
safety: No meaningful harms reported; main risk is delaying proper audiological evaluation.
bestSuitedFor: People who can't access in-person CBT, or want to start immediately
bestResult: THI −20.4 points vs sham (Japan 2026); TQ effect size d=1.1 (Kalmeda)
limitations: Most apps on the market have zero evidence — the tested few are the exception
DEFINE trial (app vs therapist) still unpublished
Several key trials are small or manufacturer-sponsored
conflicts: Kalmeda and Kyorin trials are manufacturer-involved; Oto trials are academic-company collaborations.

timeline.event: First audiologist-guided iCBT trials (Beukes, UK).
Kalmeda RCT published; permanent DiGA listing in Germany.
Oto RCT published (Flinders); DEFINE trial completes.
First double-blind sham-controlled app RCT published in JAMA Otolaryngology (Japan).

latest.text: JAMA Otolaryngology publishes a double-blind sham-controlled app RCT (N=60): THI −20.4 vs sham, 70% vs 27% meaningfully improved — small and industry-sponsored, but sham-controlled.

history.reason: Multiple positive RCTs including one sham-controlled; heterogeneous products and some industry sponsorship.

scoreRationale: Multiple independent RCT wins and a first sham-controlled success earn 3/5; the category is heterogeneous — the score applies to the tested products, not to app stores at large.

name: Cochlear implants (for qualifying hearing loss)
oneLiner: For people with severe hearing loss, implantation often genuinely reduces the tinnitus sound itself — one of the few things that does. It is never done for tinnitus alone.
whatItIs: A surgically implanted electrode array that bypasses damaged hair cells and stimulates the auditory nerve directly. Tinnitus reduction is a frequent side benefit of implantation for severe-to-profound hearing loss.
howItWorks: Restoring afferent auditory input reverses the deprivation-driven central gain and reorganization thought to generate tinnitus — the brain gets real signal again and turns the phantom down.
mechanism: Restored auditory input reducing central gain

loudness.summary: Percept-level ranges (Ramakers 2015, Laryngoscope): tinnitus decreases in 25–72% of implanted patients and is completely suppressed in 8–45% — while 0–25% experience worsening and ~9% develop new-onset tinnitus. The 2024 meta-analysis adds a pooled tinnitus VAS −3.1 (a mixed scale covering annoyance/loudness/awareness, not pure loudness).

distress.summary: Pooled within-group THI −14.0 and TQ −15.9 across 28 mostly non-randomized cohort studies (853 patients).

regulatory.detail: Cochlear implants are FDA-approved for qualifying hearing loss — not specifically for tinnitus. Tinnitus benefit is an evidence-supported secondary effect.

availability.usa: Available at implant centers for qualifying candidates; widely insurance-covered for hearing loss
availability.other: Available in most developed health systems
availability.cost: $30,000–100,000+ (typically covered by insurance for hearing-loss candidacy)

safety: Surgical risks; 0–25% experience tinnitus worsening and ~9.2% develop new-onset tinnitus after implantation (Assouly, cited in the 2024 meta-analysis).
bestSuitedFor: People who already qualify for a cochlear implant on hearing grounds
bestResult: Complete tinnitus suppression in 8–45% of implanted patients across studies
limitations: Only for implant candidates — not a general tinnitus treatment
Observational evidence; no one is implanted for tinnitus alone
Effects can wane over time; small risk of worsening

timeline.event: FDA approves the first cochlear implant; tinnitus suppression noted early.
UMC Utrecht begins an RCT of implantation for tinnitus in single-sided deafness.
Meta-analysis (28 studies, N=853): THI −14.0, loudness VAS −3.1.

latest.text: 2024 meta-analysis confirms percept-level and distress improvements after implantation.

history.reason: Consistent observational percept-level benefit in a restricted population; no RCT evidence for tinnitus as an indication.

scoreRationale: Large consistent observational literature with genuine loudness effects earns 3/5; capped because the data are non-randomized and apply only to implant candidates.
narrowNote: Applies ONLY to people who qualify for a cochlear implant because of severe-to-profound hearing loss. Nobody is implanted for tinnitus alone.

name: Hearing aids (with hearing loss)
oneLiner: If you have hearing loss with tinnitus, treating the hearing loss is one of the most effective single moves.
whatItIs: Properly fitted amplification for coexisting hearing loss — the AAO-HNSF guideline recommends a hearing aid evaluation whenever hearing loss accompanies bothersome tinnitus.
howItWorks: Amplification restores input to deprived auditory pathways (reducing the central gain that drives tinnitus), masks the tinnitus with ambient sound, and removes the strain of struggling to hear.

loudness.summary: Observational reports of reduced audibility/awareness; controlled percept-level evidence is weak.

distress.summary: In UNITI 2025 hearing aids were among the largest single-treatment effects on THI; Cochrane 2018 rates the controlled evidence as low quality.

regulatory.status: FDA regulated (hearing aids); OTC category exists
regulatory.detail: Regulated as hearing devices, not tinnitus treatments. AAO-HNSF 2014 guideline strength: 'Recommendation' (the middle tier — same as CBT; sound therapy gets only 'Option'). Since Sept 2024, Apple's AirPods Pro Hearing Aid Feature holds its own FDA De Novo authorization as OTC hearing-aid software — a $249 route to amplification for mild-moderate loss (no tinnitus-specific RCT of it exists).

availability.usa: Widely available; OTC since 2022 for mild-moderate loss
availability.europe: Widely available; publicly funded in several countries

safety: Very safe; main risk is poor fitting.
bestSuitedFor: Anyone with tinnitus plus hearing loss — get a hearing test first
bestResult: Among the largest single-treatment THI effects in UNITI (N=461)
limitations: Benefit entangled with the hearing benefit itself
Cochrane: low-quality controlled evidence
Doesn't help tinnitus with normal hearing

timeline.event: AAO-HNSF guideline recommends hearing aid evaluation for tinnitus with hearing loss.
Cochrane finds low-quality controlled evidence — the practice rests on guideline consensus.
UNITI-RCT strengthens the case: hearing aids among the top single treatments.

latest.text: UNITI-RCT: hearing aids among the largest single-treatment effect sizes.

history.reason: Guideline support plus UNITI head-to-head data, against a weak Cochrane base.

scoreRationale: Guideline recommendation and the UNITI head-to-head result earn 3/5; a trial isolating the tinnitus effect from the hearing benefit would settle it.

name: CBT for Insomnia (CBT-I)
oneLiner: Tinnitus keeps you awake; insomnia makes tinnitus worse. Treating the insomnia breaks the loop.
whatItIs: A structured insomnia therapy (sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive work) adapted for tinnitus-related insomnia. Sleep disturbance affects most people with bothersome tinnitus — estimates commonly exceed 40%.
howItWorks: Poor sleep amplifies arousal and attention to tinnitus at night; CBT-I rebuilds sleep drive and decouples bed from wakeful listening, which lowers both insomnia and tinnitus distress.
mechanism: Behavioral insomnia treatment reducing nighttime arousal

loudness.summary: No loudness effect claimed.

distress.summary: RCT (N=102): clinically meaningful insomnia improvement in >80% with CBT-I vs 47% (audiology care) and 20% (support group); tinnitus distress (a secondary outcome) also improved, sustained at 6 months.

regulatory.detail: CBT-I is first-line treatment for chronic insomnia generally.

availability.usa: Sleep clinics and digital CBT-I programs

safety: Safe; temporary daytime sleepiness during sleep restriction.
bestSuitedFor: Anyone whose tinnitus is worst at night or who dreads bedtime
bestResult: >80% vs 20% clinically meaningful insomnia improvement (vs support group)
limitations: Single-center trial
Tinnitus outcomes were secondary
Requires real behavioral commitment for several weeks

timeline.event: First adequately powered RCT of CBT-I for tinnitus-related insomnia (N=102, UCL/Barts).

latest.text: RCT: CBT-I superior to both control arms with effects sustained at 6 months; 94% completion.

history.reason: One strong RCT in a high-prevalence problem; needs replication.

scoreRationale: One well-run RCT with sustained effects earns 3/5; multicenter replication would raise it.

name: Acceptance & Commitment Therapy (ACT)
oneLiner: Stop fighting the sound — a well-supported CBT cousin built on acceptance rather than control.
whatItIs: A psychological therapy teaching acceptance of the tinnitus sensation and committed action toward valued living, rather than struggling to suppress the sound.
howItWorks: Struggling against tinnitus feeds the attention-arousal loop. ACT builds psychological flexibility — the sound stays, the fight ends, and distress falls; trial mediation analyses show acceptance drives the improvement.

loudness.summary: No loudness effect shown.

distress.summary: Meta-analysis of 3 RCTs (N=100): THI −17.7 points vs untreated controls; Westin 2011 effect size d=1.04 vs waitlist.

safety: No reported harms.
bestSuitedFor: People who feel stuck in a daily battle with the sound
bestResult: Pooled THI −17.7 (95% CI −23.5 to −11.8) vs untreated control
limitations: Small pooled sample (~100)
Fewer trials than classic CBT

timeline.event: Westin RCT: ACT beats waitlist (d=1.04) and holds up against TRT.
Meta-analysis pools 3 RCTs: THI −17.7 vs no treatment.

latest.text: ACT meta-analysis published (Indian J Otolaryngol) — consistent distress benefit.

history.reason: Consistent RCT wins but small evidence base.

scoreRationale: Meaningful pooled effect from randomized trials earns 3/5; the pooled N of ~100 keeps it from 4.

name: Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT)
oneLiner: The best-tested mindfulness approach for tinnitus — it outperformed a genuine comparison treatment (not just a waiting list), and the benefit lasted six months.
whatItIs: An 8-week group program combining mindfulness meditation with cognitive therapy, adapted for chronic tinnitus.
howItWorks: Trains non-reactive attention: tinnitus is noticed without being engaged, which weakens the appraisal-arousal loop that sustains distress. The mechanism is attention and appraisal, not loudness.

loudness.summary: Loudness ratings improved equally in both trial arms — a non-specific effect, not evidence the percept quiets.

distress.summary: MBCT beat intensity-matched active relaxation training by 6.3 TQ points post-treatment (p=0.016) and 7.2 points at 6-month follow-up (p=0.006, effect size 0.56).

availability.usa: Mindfulness programs widely available; tinnitus-specific MBCT rarer

safety: No reported harms.
bestSuitedFor: People drawn to meditation-based approaches; rumination-heavy distress
bestResult: TQ −6.3 vs active relaxation control post-treatment, −7.2 at 6-month follow-up
limitations: Evidence from specialist psychology settings
Fewer trials than CBT

timeline.event: McKenna RCT (N=75): MBCT beats relaxation training with durable effect.
Online iMBCT trial (Warsaw) underway (NCT07183826).

latest.text: Internet-delivered MBCT RCT recruiting at University of Warsaw (N=78).

history.reason: Beat an active control with persistence — rare in this field — but limited replication.

scoreRationale: Beating an active control with 6-month persistence earns 3/5; multicenter replication would raise it.

name: SPI-1005 (ebselen)
oneLiner: The most advanced drug with a tinnitus-relevant claim — but its trials are in Meniere's disease, and the tinnitus data are unblinded.
whatItIs: An oral anti-inflammatory/antioxidant (glutathione peroxidase mimetic) from Sound Pharmaceuticals, in Phase 3 for Meniere's disease with tinnitus tracked as a patient-reported outcome.
howItWorks: Mimics glutathione peroxidase to reduce oxidative stress and inflammation in the inner ear — a mechanism relevant to hearing loss, Meniere's symptoms and possibly the cochlear component of tinnitus.

loudness.summary: Company reports ≥30% patient-reported tinnitus severity improvement — from an open-label extension, so high bias risk and not a loudness measurement.

distress.summary: Same open-label PRO data; no blinded tinnitus outcome has been published.

regulatory.status: Investigational (FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation — for hearing loss in Meniere's, NOT tinnitus)
regulatory.detail: Breakthrough Therapy designation granted December 1, 2025 for treatment of hearing loss in Meniere's disease. STOPMD-3 results are company-reported; no peer-reviewed publication located as of Sept 2026. FDA publishes no BTD registry, so the sponsor announcement is the strongest available source.

safety: Reported as well tolerated in trials to date (company-reported).
bestSuitedFor: Watch-list item — Meniere's patients first, primary tinnitus later at best
bestResult: Phase 3 co-primary endpoints met (company-reported); ≥30% tinnitus PRO improvement in open-label extension
limitations: No peer-reviewed Phase 3 publication yet
Tinnitus data are open-label PROs
Indication is Meniere's, not tinnitus
conflicts: All results to date are company press releases.

timeline.event: STOPMD-3 Phase 3 topline: co-primary endpoints met (company-reported, December).
FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation (December).
Open-label Phase 3 safety study completes enrollment (July); primary completion December 2026.

latest.text: Enrollment completed in the ~200-patient open-label Phase 3 safety study (NCT06859788).

history.change: Phase 2 audit: removed from the Top 10 (was #10); replaced by rTMS
history.reason: Adversarial review: a slot on an evidence-ranked list for an agent with ZERO controlled tinnitus data (open-label, secondary outcomes, different disease) was pipeline hype — while rTMS has 29 sham-controlled RCTs showing at least short-term benefit. SPI-1005 remains a prominent watch item in the trials database.
Late-stage program but tinnitus evidence is unblinded and unpublished.

scoreRationale: A Phase 3 program with BTD earns 2/5 for tinnitus specifically: the tinnitus outcomes are open-label, company-reported, and in a Meniere's population. The ongoing Phase 3 (NCT06859788) is open-label single-group — it cannot produce controlled tinnitus evidence.
narrowNote: Studied ONLY in Meniere's disease. There is no trial of this drug in ordinary tinnitus.

name: TRTL-913 (GABA-A modulator)
oneLiner: A new $106M bet that a GABA-A drug can quiet tinnitus — Phase 2 starts soon; no human tinnitus data yet.
whatItIs: An oral GABA-A positive allosteric modulator (licensed from Hansoh) being developed for tinnitus by Tortugas Neuroscience, which launched in April 2026 with $106M.
howItWorks: Tinnitus involves reduced inhibitory (GABAergic) tone in central auditory circuits; enhancing GABA-A signaling aims to restore inhibition and damp the hyperactivity generating the phantom sound.
mechanism: GABA-A positive allosteric modulation (restoring central inhibition)

loudness.summary: No human tinnitus data yet.

distress.summary: No human tinnitus data yet.

regulatory.detail: NCT07777549: Phase 2, N=100, not yet recruiting; estimated completion August 2027. One of only two Phase 2+ drug trials with tinnitus as the primary indication.

subtypes: to be defined by the trial
safety: Unknown in tinnitus populations; GABA-A drugs generally carry sedation/dependence considerations.
bestSuitedFor: Watch-list item only
bestResult: None yet — first tinnitus trial pending
limitations: Zero human tinnitus data
History is against tinnitus drugs: every rigorously placebo-controlled candidate so far has failed

timeline.event: Tortugas Neuroscience launches with $106M (April); Phase 2 tinnitus trial registered.

latest.text: Tortugas launches with four Phase 2-stage neuro assets including TRTL-913 for tinnitus.

history.reason: Credible mechanism and funding; no human evidence.

scoreRationale: Score 1/5: nothing but mechanism and money so far — which is exactly what the ranking rules say cannot earn a high score.

name: Physiotherapy & TMJ treatment (somatic tinnitus)
oneLiner: When tinnitus changes with your jaw or neck, treating the jaw or neck can change the tinnitus.
whatItIs: Physical therapy for the neck, TMJ (jaw) treatment, and musculoskeletal care for somatosensory tinnitus — the subtype where head/neck signals modulate the sound. Roughly 60–80% of tinnitus patients can modulate their tinnitus somewhat with jaw or neck maneuvers (Ralli 2016: 79.7% in TMJ/neck patients; Lee 2020: 61.7% in a general clinic; Sanchez & Rocha 2011 review: ~65%). Note: chiropractic/osteopathic manipulation adds no evidence over exercise-based physiotherapy, and high-velocity neck manipulation carries a rare but serious artery-dissection risk.
howItWorks: Somatosensory nerves from the jaw and upper neck converge on the dorsal cochlear nucleus, the same circuit implicated in tinnitus generation. Abnormal muscle or joint input can drive the percept; treating it can reduce the drive.
mechanism: Reducing aberrant somatosensory input to the dorsal cochlear nucleus

loudness.summary: Somatic maneuvers demonstrably change the percept's loudness/pitch; after TMJ-disorder treatment, 43% had decreased tinnitus at 2 years vs 12% of waiting-list controls (Tullberg & Ernberg 2006, PMID 16546850, p<0.001).

distress.summary: Supervised physiotherapy programs improved severity in controlled studies; no large multicenter RCT yet.

subtypes: tinnitus with TMJ disorder or neck dysfunction
safety: Safe with qualified providers; avoid aggressive or expensive unproven dental interventions.
bestSuitedFor: People whose tinnitus changes with jaw clenching, neck movement or posture
bestResult: 43% vs 12% decreased tinnitus 2 years after TMJ-disorder treatment
limitations: Subtype definitions vary — prevalence numbers are inconsistent
No large multicenter RCT (VA trial NCT05434637 running, due 2027)

extraSources.title: Tullberg & Ernberg 2006, Acta Odontol Scand — TMJ treatment 2-year follow-up (43% vs 12%)

timeline.event: TMJ-treatment 2-year follow-up: 43% vs 12% improved (Tullberg & Ernberg).
Controlled study: supervised physiotherapy improves somatic tinnitus severity.
VA somatosensory tinnitus RCT (N=72) recruiting.

latest.text: VA somatosensory RCT continues recruiting; UCLH 'somatic tracking' attention trial also active.

history.reason: Mechanistically grounded with controlled but small evidence.

scoreRationale: Real percept modulation and positive controlled studies earn 2/5; a proper multicenter RCT would move it.

name: Sound therapy & masking
oneLiner: Widely used, low-risk, valued by many — but never proven better than placebo in controlled trials.
whatItIs: Background sound — noise, nature sounds, music, sound generators or apps — used to partially cover tinnitus, ease its intrusiveness, and help sleep and focus.
howItWorks: External sound reduces the contrast between tinnitus and silence, gives the auditory system real input to process, and supports habituation. It manages the experience rather than changing the tinnitus.
mechanism: Partial masking / contrast reduction / habituation support

loudness.summary: No controlled evidence that sound therapy durably reduces the percept. Newer music-therapy meta-analyses report loudness improvements, but from low-quality trials.

distress.summary: Cochrane 2018: NO usable trial data exist for sound therapy vs waitlist/placebo/information — the central question has simply never been answered; the 8 trials (N=590) only compared device types, with no differences found. Guideline status: 'Option'. Many individuals still find it genuinely helpful day to day.

regulatory.detail: AAO-HNSF 2014 lists sound therapy as an option (benefit/harm balance, medium-quality evidence).

availability.usa: Free apps to clinical sound generators

safety: Very safe at comfortable volumes; keep sound below or at the tinnitus level rather than drowning it out.
bestSuitedFor: Sleep-time relief, quiet-environment comfort, first self-help step
bestResult: Individual preference effects are real; group-level superiority unproven
limitations: The sound-therapy-vs-placebo question has never produced usable trial data (absence of evidence, not proof of no effect)
Effects end when the sound stops
Commercial products often oversell the science

timeline.event: First 'masking' descriptions in the literature.
Cochrane: no superiority over placebo demonstrated.
TRTT: sound generators added nothing measurable over counseling.

latest.text: Music-therapy meta-analysis (14 studies, N=1,239) reports THI and loudness improvements — evidence quality remains low.

history.reason: Safe and widely valued; unproven vs placebo.

scoreRationale: Ubiquitous and safe but never separated from placebo in quality trials: 2/5, Tier 4 (coping/symptom management).

name: Tinnitus Retraining Therapy (TRT)
oneLiner: The counseling helps — but the trial designed to prove TRT found its sound generators added nothing.
whatItIs: A structured program combining directive counseling with low-level sound generators, aiming for habituation over 12–24 months.
howItWorks: Counseling reframes tinnitus as neutral; constant low-level sound is supposed to aid subconscious habituation. The TRTT trial suggests the counseling carries the benefit.
mechanism: Habituation via counseling (+ sound enrichment of unproven added value)

loudness.summary: No loudness effect shown.

distress.summary: All TRTT arms improved substantially (~77.5% achieved meaningful TQ reduction) — but TRT showed no advantage over standard care.

availability.cost: $2,000–5,000 for a full program incl. devices

safety: Safe.
bestSuitedFor: People who want a structured audiologist-led program — knowing CBT has better evidence
bestResult: Large within-group improvement in TRTT; no between-group advantage
limitations: TRTT: no meaningful advantage over standard care
Long, expensive protocol
CBT beat TRT directly in one trial

timeline.event: Jastreboff's neurophysiological model launches TRT.
TRTT (N=151): TRT no better than standard of care at 18 months.

latest.text: Follow-up analyses attribute TRTT benefit mainly to counseling, not sound generators.

history.reason: Counseling component works; the distinctive TRT elements failed their definitive test.

scoreRationale: Its own definitive trial found no advantage over standard care: 2/5, Tier 4.

name: rTMS (repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation)
oneLiner: Statistically real but clinically small — and whether any benefit lasts to 6 months is disputed between the major analyses.
whatItIs: Magnetic pulses applied over auditory/prefrontal cortex in clinic sessions, usually daily for 1–4 weeks. FDA-cleared TMS systems exist for depression/OCD; tinnitus use is off-label/investigational.
howItWorks: Aims to reduce the cortical hyperactivity and maladaptive plasticity underlying tinnitus by repeatedly stimulating (usually inhibiting) auditory cortex.

loudness.summary: Loudness/psychoacoustic effects inconsistent; 2020 meta-analysis found no significant effect on loudness measures.

distress.summary: Beats sham in the weeks after treatment (2025 meta: THI −11.5 post, −11.0 at 1 month across 16 RCTs). At 6 months the meta-analyses DISAGREE: 2020 (29 RCTs) found a small significant effect (−6.53), 2025 found none (−4.26, NS) — and even the significant estimates sit at/below the ~7-point meaningfulness threshold.

regulatory.detail: No TMS system carries a tinnitus indication; AAO-HNSF 2014 recommends against routine TMS for tinnitus.

availability.usa: Off-label at some centers; research settings

safety: Generally safe; rare seizure risk; scalp discomfort and headache common.
bestSuitedFor: Research participation; short-term relief expectations only
bestResult: THI −11.5 vs sham post-treatment (2025 pooled estimate)
limitations: 6-month durability disputed between meta-analyses; effect sizes at/below clinical meaningfulness
Huge protocol heterogeneity
Guideline recommends against routine use

timeline.event: First tinnitus rTMS trials.
AAO-HNSF recommends against routine rTMS.
Meta-analysis of 16 RCTs: short-term benefit only.

latest.text: Frontiers meta-analysis: effect at 1 month, none at 6 months. Navigated-rTMS and personalized-target trials now recruiting.

history.change: Phase 2 audit: added to the Top 10 at #10 (replacing SPI-1005)
history.reason: By volume of controlled evidence, rTMS (29 sham-controlled RCTs, N=1,228) outranks a drug with zero controlled tinnitus data. Framed honestly: consistent short-term sham-controlled benefit; durability disputed; not guideline-recommended.
Real but small, non-durable effects.

scoreRationale: Many RCTs but small effects at/below clinical meaningfulness, disputed durability, and guideline advice against routine use: 2/5.

name: tDCS / tACS / tRNS (transcranial electrical stimulation)
oneLiner: Cheap and safe, possibly a mild adjunct — the evidence is too heterogeneous to say more.
whatItIs: Weak electrical currents applied to the scalp (direct, alternating, or random-noise), in clinic or via emerging home-use protocols. tRNS has only small pilot studies (a 2024 systematic review of 7 calls it 'promising' but unproven). At the invasive extreme, deep brain stimulation for tinnitus exists only as tiny case series (a caudate Phase 1 of 6 patients) and a 7-patient Grenoble trial.
howItWorks: Shifts cortical excitability under the electrodes; temporal-lobe montages target auditory circuits, prefrontal montages target the distress network.

loudness.summary: 2022 meta-analysis: significant loudness reduction only with lateral-temporal stimulation, small-to-moderate effect.

distress.summary: Prefrontal stimulation mainly improved comorbid depression/anxiety; verdict — possible adjunct, not standalone.

regulatory.detail: No FDA authorization for tinnitus.

availability.europe: Research (UK WHITBY home-tDCS feasibility trial running)
availability.cost: Low per-session cost in research; consumer devices unproven

safety: Very safe at standard parameters; skin tingling.
bestSuitedFor: Research participation
bestResult: Small-to-moderate pooled effects, montage-dependent
limitations: Protocol heterogeneity blocks conclusions
No durable-benefit evidence

timeline.event: Meta-analysis: possible adjunct role; Brain publishes large dual-site RCT.
WHITBY home-based tDCS feasibility trial (Nottingham) due to complete.

latest.text: WHITBY feasibility trial (N=40) approaching primary completion.

history.reason: Mixed, low-certainty evidence.

scoreRationale: Small effects in heterogeneous trials: 2/5.

name: Paired vagus nerve stimulation (VNS)
oneLiner: A promising pilot, then silence — the sponsor took the technology to stroke rehab instead.
whatItIs: An implanted vagus nerve stimulator delivering pulses precisely paired with tones, intended to drive targeted auditory-cortex plasticity (MicroTransponder Serenity system).
howItWorks: VNS bursts release plasticity-promoting neuromodulators; pairing them with specific tones aims to remap auditory cortex away from the tinnitus frequency.

loudness.summary: No verified loudness-percept reduction data.

distress.summary: Pilot RCT: 50% meaningful THI improvement vs 28% control at 6 weeks, concentrated in tonal, non-blast tinnitus.

regulatory.detail: Never authorized for tinnitus. The paired-VNS platform received FDA PMA approval as Vivistim (P210007, approved 2021-08-27) — for stroke upper-limb rehabilitation; the PMA applicant of record is now Mobia Medical, Inc. (successor to MicroTransponder).

safety: Requires surgery; VNS implant risks.
bestSuitedFor: Nobody currently — program dormant
bestResult: 50% vs 28% meaningful THI improvement (pilot, N=30)
limitations: Invasive
No development since ~2017
Pilot-scale evidence only

timeline.event: Randomized double-blind pilot published.
Sponsor pivots platform to stroke rehab (Vivistim PMA).

latest.text: Vivistim PMA for stroke — tinnitus program effectively shelved.

history.reason: Positive pilot, dormant program.

scoreRationale: A single positive pilot with no follow-through: 2/5, dormant.

name: Neosensory Duo (wristband bimodal)
oneLiner: A consumer wristband borrowing the bimodal idea — sold on one small company-run study.
whatItIs: A vibrating wristband paired with tone playback from an app (10 minutes/day), sold directly to consumers as a wellness device.
howItWorks: Claims the bimodal principle: pairing tones with synchronized skin vibration to drive auditory-circuit plasticity — via the wrist rather than tongue or neck.

loudness.summary: No loudness data.

distress.summary: One company-run study: TFI −17.9 in the experimental group — unblinded, no sham vibration, all authors are company employees.

regulatory.status: Consumer wellness device (no FDA authorization found)
regulatory.detail: Sold as general wellness; no FDA clearance/authorization for tinnitus treatment located.

safety: Benign (vibration + sound).
bestSuitedFor: Consumers who accept wellness-tier evidence
bestResult: TFI −17.9 (company study, unblinded)
limitations: Single small manufacturer-run study in a minor journal
No sham control — participants knew their group
Wrist stimulation lacks the anatomical rationale of tongue/neck approaches
conflicts: All study authors are Neosensory employees or its founder/CEO.

timeline.event: Company announces wristband tinnitus results.
Study published in International Tinnitus Journal.

latest.text: Company active; distribution partnership announced. No new controlled evidence.

history.reason: One unblinded company study.

scoreRationale: Marketing currently exceeds evidence: 1/5 until independent controlled data exist.

name: Acoustic coordinated reset (Desyncra)
oneLiner: A elegant theory whose confirmatory trial came back empty.
whatItIs: Patterned tone sequences around the tinnitus frequency intended to 'desynchronize' pathological neural firing (coordinated reset), delivered via a proprietary device.
howItWorks: Theory: brief tones at staggered frequencies break up synchronized firing in tinnitus-generating networks. The controlled RESET2 trial failed to confirm a benefit.

loudness.summary: The definitive independent double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Hall 2022, N=100) found no benefit over placebo.

distress.summary: Hall 2022: primary outcome (Tinnitus Handicap Questionnaire at 12 weeks) p=0.85 vs placebo.

regulatory.status: FDA 510(k)-cleared as a tinnitus MASKER (K112752); commercially inactive
regulatory.detail: The T30 CR device was cleared in 2011 under the masker regulation (874.3400) — clearance is not efficacy. A 2017 systematic review already called the evidence insufficient; the independent 2022 RCT was null. Current company status could not be verified.

safety: Benign sound exposure.
bestSuitedFor: Nobody currently
bestResult: Positive 2012 pilot — refuted by the independent 2022 placebo-controlled trial
limitations: Independent double-blind RCT (N=100) was null (p=0.85)
Proprietary and expensive when sold
conflicts: Original program manufacturer-linked; the null 2022 trial was independent (NIHR Nottingham).

timeline.event: T30 device FDA 510(k)-cleared as a tinnitus masker (K112752).
Positive pilot RCT published.
Industry-co-authored evaluation calls RESET2 'non-conclusive'; systematic review says insufficient evidence.
Independent double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Hall et al., N=100): no benefit over placebo.

history.reason: Failed confirmatory trial.

scoreRationale: The definitive test failed: 1/5, Tier 5.

name: Notched sound / notched music therapy
oneLiner: Music with your tinnitus frequency carved out — a modest, unconfirmed loudness effect in tonal tinnitus.
whatItIs: Music or noise filtered to remove a band around your tinnitus frequency, listened to for hours daily over months (tailor-made notched music training, TMNMT).
howItWorks: Lateral inhibition theory: neurons around the notch suppress those inside it, potentially reducing the over-representation of the tinnitus frequency.
mechanism: Lateral inhibition at the tinnitus frequency

loudness.summary: Münster trials: modest effects mainly on perceived loudness in tonal tinnitus; notch width didn't matter.

distress.summary: Independent RCT (N=104, 6 months): THI difference 7.2 points favoring notched music — not statistically significant.

safety: Safe at comfortable volume.
bestSuitedFor: Tonal tinnitus, patient people (months of daily listening)
bestResult: Modest loudness reduction in tonal tinnitus (Münster)
limitations: Larger controlled comparisons failed to reach significance
Requires precise pitch matching and long adherence

timeline.event: Münster proof-of-concept published (PNAS).
Independent RCT: no significant THI benefit vs ordinary music.

latest.text: Newcastle University (Sedley/Yukhnovich, RNID-funded, N=77) reported a desynchronizing sound-therapy variant producing ~10% loudness reduction lasting ~3 weeks — an emerging cousin of the notched approach.
New notched-vs-conventional-music comparison published (Eur Arch ORL); verdict still 'promising but unproven'.

history.reason: Mixed results; small possible loudness effect.

scoreRationale: A plausible mechanism with mixed trials: 2/5.

name: Combination aids & fractal tones (e.g., Widex Zen)
oneLiner: Hearing aids with built-in tinnitus sounds — sensible, but the tinnitus add-ons lack independent proof.
whatItIs: Hearing aids that also play masking sounds or generative 'fractal' chime-like tones (Widex Zen being the best-known), usually within a counseling program.
howItWorks: Combines amplification benefits with sound enrichment; fractal tones aim to be pleasant and unpredictable enough not to be memorized.

loudness.summary: No controlled loudness evidence.

distress.summary: Peer-reviewed evidence is tiny: Sweetow & Sabes 2010 (N=14, manufacturer-affiliated) reported clinically significant improvement in over half of participants; an independent 6-patient pilot found a 20-point THI drop. Larger '~30-point' claims trace to trade articles, not peer review. Cochrane found insufficient evidence that combination aids beat plain hearing aids.

safety: Safe.
bestSuitedFor: People getting hearing aids anyway who want built-in sound options
bestResult: THI −20 in a 6-patient independent pilot; N=14 manufacturer study reports 'clinically significant' improvement in over half
limitations: No independent RCTs of the tinnitus features
Cochrane: no proven advantage over plain hearing aids
Trade-press claims exceed the peer-reviewed numbers

extraSources.title: Sweetow & Sabes 2010, J Am Acad Audiol (N=14) — PMID 20807482
Simonetti et al. 2018, Int Arch Otorhinolaryngol (N=6 pilot) — PMID 30357067

timeline.event: Widex Zen Therapy program introduced.
Cochrane: combination devices unproven vs alternatives.

history.reason: Reasonable option inside hearing-aid care; unproven add-on value.

scoreRationale: The hearing-aid core is sound; the tinnitus-specific claims are manufacturer-backed only: 2/5.

name: TrueSilence / digital polytherapeutic (Searchfield)
oneLiner: Thirty years of Auckland tinnitus research just became a startup — personalized, gamified sound therapy by phone.
whatItIs: A clinician-guided 90-day smartphone program (QCore platform) combining personalized passive and active sound therapy and training games, from Grant Searchfield's University of Auckland group; spun out as TrueSilence Therapeutics in August 2026.
howItWorks: 'Polytherapeutic' approach: matches sound therapy to the individual and adds attention-training elements, on the theory that tinnitus is partly a disorder of auditory attention and adaptation.

loudness.summary: No loudness claims verified.

distress.summary: The 2022 prototype RCT (single-blind, N=61 analyzed): TFI −17.8 vs −10.1 with a white-noise app; clinically meaningful response 65% vs 43%. No product-level trials of the commercial version yet.

regulatory.status: Early commercial (regulatory status not yet established)
regulatory.detail: Company (Atlanta-based, technical staff in NZ) launched August 2026, rolling out via NZ audiologists while pursuing US regulatory approval. The launch is company news, not new clinical evidence.

availability.usa: Rolling out via app + earbuds model

safety: Benign (sound + games).
bestSuitedFor: Watch-list item as the product launches
bestResult: Prototype RCT: TFI −17.8 vs −10.1 (white-noise app), 65% vs 43% responders
limitations: Commercial product is new; evidence is for the research prototype
Single-group research lineage; completer-only analysis in the prototype trial

extraSources.title: University of Auckland — How 30 years of tinnitus research became a start-up (Aug 2026)

timeline.event: Digital polytherapeutic RCT published (Frontiers in Neurology).
TrueSilence Therapeutics spinout announced (August).

latest.text: University of Auckland announces the TrueSilence Therapeutics spinout delivering the QCore platform.

history.reason: Promising research lineage, product-stage evidence pending.

scoreRationale: Respected research lineage with one supportive RCT for the prototype: 2/5 pending product-level trials.

name: Intratympanic drug injections
oneLiner: Injections through the eardrum keep failing their controlled tests — the placebo response is doing the work.
whatItIs: Steroids, lidocaine or experimental drugs injected through the eardrum into the middle ear. Two of the largest placebo-controlled programs in tinnitus history used this route — and both failed.
howItWorks: Delivers drug directly to the round window for inner-ear absorption. The rationale is sound; the controlled results are not.

loudness.summary: AM-101/TACTT2 failed its loudness endpoint; lidocaine's transient suppression lasts minutes and causes vertigo.

distress.summary: OTO-313: placebo beat drug numerically (36% vs 26% TFI responders). TACTT3 (N=893) failed its TFI endpoint. Positive results come only from small trials without placebo arms.

regulatory.detail: AAO-HNSF 2014 recommends against routine intratympanic drugs for tinnitus.

safety: Eardrum perforation risk, pain, transient vertigo (especially lidocaine).
bestSuitedFor: Not supported for tinnitus outside trials
bestResult: None in placebo-controlled trials
limitations: Both large placebo-controlled programs failed
30–40% placebo responder rates explain the open-label 'wins'

timeline.event: TACTT2 Phase 3 fails (loudness endpoint).
TACTT3 Phase 3 fails (TFI endpoint); sponsor exits otology.
OTO-313 Phase 2 fails; Otonomy dissolves.

latest.text: Pipeline note: AudioCure's AC102 (intratympanic pyridoindole) is in Phase 2 for sudden hearing loss with tinnitus outcomes — preclinical tinnitus claims, no controlled human tinnitus data yet.
OTO-313 negative trial published in peer review — placebo numerically superior.

history.reason: Repeated controlled failures.

scoreRationale: The best-controlled data in the field are negative: 1/5, Tier 5.

name: Off-label oral drugs (antidepressants, benzodiazepines, gabapentin, betahistine)
oneLiner: No drug is approved for tinnitus anywhere — and the systematic reviews say none of the usual suspects works on the tinnitus itself.
whatItIs: Commonly prescribed medications used off-label: tricyclics/SSRIs, benzodiazepines, anticonvulsants (gabapentin), betahistine and others. There is no FDA- or EMA-approved drug for tinnitus.
howItWorks: Various CNS mechanisms; in practice, any benefit usually reflects treatment of comorbid depression, anxiety or insomnia rather than the tinnitus percept.

loudness.summary: No drug has shown a loudness effect in a confirmatory trial.

distress.summary: Antidepressants can help comorbid depression/anxiety; Cochrane finds tricyclics no better than placebo for tinnitus severity; insufficient evidence for benzodiazepines; gabapentin ineffective; betahistine — 'absence of evidence'.

regulatory.status: No drug approved for tinnitus (all use off-label)
regulatory.detail: AAO-HNSF 2014 recommends against routine antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics and intratympanic drugs for tinnitus.

safety: Real side-effect burdens — benzodiazepine dependence, anticholinergic effects, sedation. Weigh against absent tinnitus benefit.
bestSuitedFor: Treating genuine comorbid depression, anxiety or insomnia — not the tinnitus
bestResult: None on tinnitus-specific outcomes in quality trials
limitations: 2025 network meta-analysis: 78% of drug trials have methodological concerns; evidence low to very low

timeline.event: Neramexane Phase 3 fails; program abandoned (~2012).
Guideline recommends against routine drug therapy.
AUT00063 (Kv3) terminated for futility.
Network meta-analysis of 60 RCTs: no approved drug, weak evidence base.

latest.text: BMJ Open network meta-analysis reaffirms: no approved pharmacotherapy; evidence low to very low.

history.reason: Systematic reviews consistently negative for tinnitus-specific benefit.

scoreRationale: Half a century of trials without a single confirmatory win: 1/5 for tinnitus itself (comorbidity treatment is a separate, legitimate decision).

name: Supplements (ginkgo, zinc, melatonin…)
oneLiner: Heavily marketed, repeatedly tested, consistently unsupported.
whatItIs: Over-the-counter products marketed for tinnitus — Ginkgo biloba, zinc, melatonin, B vitamins, magnesium and branded blends.
howItWorks: Claimed circulation/antioxidant/neural mechanisms; none validated for tinnitus.

loudness.summary: No effect shown.

distress.summary: Cochrane on ginkgo (12 studies, N=1,915): 'little to no effect', very uncertain. Cochrane on zinc: no evidence of benefit. Melatonin: small studies suggest sleep benefit at best — not a tinnitus effect.

regulatory.detail: AAO-HNSF 2014 recommends against dietary supplements for tinnitus. Marketing claims on these products routinely exceed all evidence.

safety: Ginkgo has bleeding-risk interactions; zinc excess causes copper deficiency. 'Natural' is not 'harmless'.
bestSuitedFor: Nobody, for tinnitus. Melatonin may modestly help sleep.
bestResult: None in quality trials
limitations: Marketing vastly exceeds evidence
Ongoing cost with no expected benefit
conflicts: Supplement-industry-funded studies are common in this space.

timeline.event: Cochrane: zinc — no evidence of benefit.
Cochrane: ginkgo — little to no effect.

history.reason: Cochrane-level negative evidence.

scoreRationale: Multiple Cochrane reviews found nothing: 1/5, Tier 5 — the clearest marketing-vs-evidence gap on the site.

name: Hair-cell regeneration & inner-ear gene therapy
oneLiner: Gene therapy is genuinely restoring hearing in deaf children — but nothing in the regenerative pipeline measures tinnitus yet.
whatItIs: The long-horizon hope: regrow or repair the damaged inner-ear cells whose loss drives most tinnitus. Includes hair-cell regeneration drugs (FX-322 — failed), gene therapy (DB-OTO, AK-OTOF — succeeding, for congenital deafness), and neural-progenitor cell therapy (Rinri — first-in-human).
howItWorks: If hearing loss deprives the brain of input and the brain compensates with the phantom of tinnitus, restoring genuine input might switch the phantom off. Clinically unproven either way — no regenerative program has tinnitus as an endpoint.
mechanism: Restoring cochlear input (hair cells, synapses, nerve, or gene function)

loudness.summary: No clinical tinnitus data from any regenerative program.

distress.summary: Same.

regulatory.detail: DB-OTO (Regeneron): 11 of 12 deaf children gained hearing, 3 to normal thresholds — NEJM 2025; congenital OTOF deafness, not tinnitus. FX-322/FX-345 discontinued Feb 2023 after Phase 2b failure. Rinri's Rincell-1 first-in-human approved by UK MHRA 2025.

safety: DB-OTO: no therapy-related serious adverse events reported to date.
bestSuitedFor: The long watch — this is where a real cure could eventually come from
bestResult: Hearing restoration in OTOF children (platform proof, not a tinnitus result)
limitations: No tinnitus endpoints anywhere in the pipeline
FX-322's failure shows regeneration in adults is far harder than gene replacement in children
Whether restoring input reverses established central tinnitus is an open question

extraSources.title: Rinri Therapeutics — first-in-human cell therapy approved (Sheffield, 2025)

timeline.event: FX-322 Phase 2b fails; Frequency Therapeutics exits hearing (Feb).
AK-OTOF restores hearing in first participant (Lilly/Akouos).
DB-OTO CHORD results published in NEJM; Rinri first-in-human approved.

latest.text: DB-OTO: 11/12 children improved, 3 reached normal hearing thresholds (NEJM 2025).

history.reason: Platform succeeding in adjacent indications; zero tinnitus data.

scoreRationale: Scored for tinnitus specifically: 1/5 (no data), Tier 3 as a legitimate emerging field to watch.

name: Venous sinus stenting (pulsatile tinnitus)
oneLiner: Pulsatile tinnitus is a different disease — and when a venous narrowing is the cause, stenting resolves it in most patients.
whatItIs: For PULSATILE tinnitus (a rhythmic whooshing in time with the heartbeat, ~4% of tinnitus), imaging can reveal a physical cause — most treatably, transverse/sigmoid sinus stenosis. A stent placed in the narrowed vein eliminates the turbulent flow generating the sound.
howItWorks: Narrowed dural venous sinuses create turbulent, audible blood flow near the inner ear. Stenting restores smooth flow, removing the sound at its physical source — this is cause-removal, not symptom management.
mechanism: Eliminating turbulent venous flow at its source

loudness.summary: In correctly selected venous-stenosis patients, pooled analysis of 28 studies (N=616): 91.7% improvement and 88.6% complete resolution of the pulsatile sound. This is elimination of the percept — in a specific, imaging-confirmed subgroup.

distress.summary: Distress resolves with the sound; measured mostly as symptom resolution rather than THI/TFI.

regulatory.status: Off-label use of approved stents; dedicated device investigational
regulatory.detail: Venous stents are used off-label for pulsatile tinnitus; a dedicated device (BosSTENT, Sonorous NV) is in a 90-patient trial (NCT07070089).

availability.usa: Neurointerventional centers, after full imaging workup
availability.cost: Procedure-level costs; often covered when medically indicated

subtypes: pulsatile tinnitus with imaging-confirmed venous sinus stenosis ONLY
safety: Real procedural risks (vessel injury, in-stent stenosis, antiplatelet therapy); requires an experienced neurointerventional team.
bestSuitedFor: Pulsatile tinnitus with confirmed venous sinus stenosis — see a physician for imaging; never assume
bestResult: 88.6% complete resolution (pooled, N=616)
limitations: Observational evidence only — no RCT yet
Applies to one imaging-confirmed cause, not pulsatile tinnitus generally
Any new pulsatile tinnitus needs medical evaluation first — some causes are dangerous

timeline.event: Pooled analysis of 28 studies (N=616): ~90% resolution in venous-stenosis pulsatile tinnitus.
Dedicated stent (BosSTENT) 90-patient trial registered.

latest.text: BosSTENT dedicated-device trial (N=90) registered (NCT07070089).

history.change: Added in Phase 2 audit: Tier 2, evidence score 3/5
history.reason: Closes the platform's subjective-only blind spot; strong observational resolution rates in a defined subgroup.

scoreRationale: Consistent ~90% resolution across 28 observational studies earns 3/5; no RCT and strict subgroup applicability cap it there.
narrowNote: Studied ONLY in pulsatile tinnitus with an imaging-confirmed venous sinus narrowing. Pulsatile tinnitus means a rhythmic whooshing in time with your heartbeat — if your tinnitus is a steady tone or hiss, this page is not about your tinnitus, and the ~90% resolution rates do not apply.

name: Transcutaneous auricular VNS (taVNS)
oneLiner: Non-surgical vagus nerve stimulation via an ear clip — small pilots so far, with the largest trial ever now running.
whatItIs: Electrical stimulation of the vagus nerve's auricular branch through a clip on the tragus/concha, alone or paired with sound (e.g., notched music) — the non-invasive cousin of the implanted paired-VNS approach. Cheap consumer ear-clip stimulators are already sold online.
howItWorks: Vagal stimulation releases plasticity-promoting neuromodulators; pairing it with sound aims to steer auditory-circuit plasticity — same theory as implanted paired VNS, without surgery.

loudness.summary: No convincing percept-level data.

distress.summary: Systematic reviews (2023) find only small heterogeneous pilots — insufficient evidence.

regulatory.status: Investigational for tinnitus; consumer devices unregulated
regulatory.detail: No FDA clearance/authorization for tinnitus. Sun Yat-Sen Memorial Hospital runs a multicenter double-blind RCT of taVNS + notched music (NCT05417711), with a larger successor registered — the biggest taVNS tinnitus program to date.

safety: Generally well tolerated; local skin irritation; consumer devices vary in quality.
bestSuitedFor: Research participation — consumer devices are unproven
bestResult: Pilot-level signals only
limitations: Only small heterogeneous pilots published
Consumer devices sold well ahead of the evidence

timeline.event: Systematic review: evidence insufficient; Sun Yat-Sen double-blind RCT begins.

latest.text: Large multicenter taVNS + notched-music program continues; successor trial registered.

history.change: Added in Phase 2 audit: Tier 3, evidence score 2/5
history.reason: Completes the VNS/bimodal family; users conflate it with Lenire and implanted VNS.

scoreRationale: Plausible mechanism, pilots only: 2/5 pending the running double-blind RCT.

name: Levo System (sleep-time sound matching)
oneLiner: FDA-cleared sound therapy played during sleep, matched to your tinnitus 'sound print' — one small positive trial.
whatItIs: An iPad-based system (Otoharmonics) that builds a match of your tinnitus sound and plays it through custom earbuds while you sleep; fitted through audiology clinics and distributed in the VA.
howItWorks: Presenting a stimulus matched to the tinnitus during sleep aims to promote habituation/adaptation to the specific percept.

loudness.summary: In the N=60 VA trial, the sound-match arm had the greatest reduction in rated tinnitus intensity — small study, no long-term data.

distress.summary: TFI improved most in the sound-match arm (Theodoroff 2017).

regulatory.detail: Cleared as a tinnitus-masking/sound-therapy device (2014) — clearance means substantial equivalence to earlier maskers, not proven efficacy.

safety: Benign sound exposure.
bestSuitedFor: People offered it through the VA; others should weigh cost vs one small trial
bestResult: Greatest intensity + TFI improvement vs comparators in an N=60 RCT
limitations: Single small RCT, sponsor-linked
No long-term or independent replication

timeline.event: FDA 510(k) clearance (K140845).
VA Portland RCT (N=60) published.

howItWorks: Ultrasound can modulate neural activity in deep structures (e.g., striatal targets implicated by DBS case series) without surgery — precision rTMS cannot reach.

loudness.summary: No human tinnitus data yet.

distress.summary: No human tinnitus data yet.

regulatory.detail: Research-stage only.

developer: University of Oxford / Tinnitus Quest funding
safety: Unknown for this application; low-intensity protocols generally well tolerated in other indications.
bestSuitedFor: Watch-list item only
bestResult: None yet
limitations: No human tinnitus data of any kind

name: Biofeedback & EEG neurofeedback
oneLiner: Clinics sell it at high cost; the best trial found the specific 'brain training' doesn't matter — the coping does.
whatItIs: Training to control physiological signals (muscle tension, skin conductance) or EEG rhythms, offered by biofeedback and neurofeedback clinics for tinnitus.
howItWorks: Biofeedback-assisted relaxation reduces arousal (a real CBT-adjacent mechanism). EEG neurofeedback claims to normalize specific tinnitus-related brain rhythms — the specificity claim is what failed testing.

loudness.summary: The 2023 Brain Communications RCT found both opposite neurofeedback protocols reduced intensity ratings equally — a non-specific effect, with no THI benefit.

distress.summary: Biofeedback-based CBT had one good RCT (Weise 2008, N=130, distress benefit maintained 6 months) — but the active ingredient is the CBT.

safety: Benign; the risk is financial.
bestSuitedFor: If relaxation training appeals — but CBT delivers the same ingredient with better evidence
bestResult: Weise 2008 biofeedback-CBT: durable distress reduction (N=130)
limitations: Definitive neurofeedback RCT showed protocol-nonspecific effects and no THI benefit
Expensive multi-session courses

timeline.event: Biofeedback-based CBT RCT (N=130) shows durable distress benefit.

name: Acupuncture
oneLiner: The world's most-used complementary tinnitus treatment — low-quality trials say yes, higher-quality analysis says unproven.
whatItIs: Needle-based treatment from traditional Chinese medicine; among the most commonly tried complementary approaches for tinnitus worldwide, with dozens of (mostly Chinese) RCTs.
howItWorks: Proposed mechanisms (local circulation, neuromodulation) remain unvalidated for tinnitus.

loudness.summary: 2020 systematic review/meta-analysis (18 RCTs): no significant effect on the primary VAS outcome vs control.

distress.summary: A 2022 umbrella review of systematic reviews rated all of them methodologically low quality: positive results 'must be viewed with caution'.

safety: Generally safe with licensed practitioners (minor bruising; rare infections).
bestSuitedFor: Not supported for tinnitus; if tried, cap the spend and timeline in advance
bestResult: Positive results only in low-quality, unblinded trials
limitations: Positive trials are low-quality and unblinded; sham-controlled results are null
Publication bias documented in this literature

name: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT)
oneLiner: Oxygen chambers are sold for tinnitus at hundreds of dollars a session; Cochrane says routine use 'cannot be justified'.
whatItIs: Breathing 100% oxygen at above-atmospheric pressure in a chamber; marketed by private hyperbaric clinics for tinnitus and sudden hearing loss.
howItWorks: Claimed to improve cochlear oxygenation. For chronic tinnitus there is no evidence the mechanism helps.
mechanism: Increased oxygen delivery (unproven benefit for chronic tinnitus)

loudness.summary: Cochrane (7 RCTs, N=392): significance of any tinnitus improvement 'could not be assessed'; no benefit for tinnitus present over 6 months.

distress.summary: Same review: small, methodologically poor studies; routine use not justified.

regulatory.status: FDA-regulated chambers; tinnitus is NOT an approved indication

safety: Barotrauma risk, temporary myopia, oxygen toxicity at extremes; plus significant cost.
bestSuitedFor: Nobody with chronic tinnitus, per Cochrane
bestResult: None assessable in quality trials
limitations: Cochrane: small, poor studies; benefit unassessable

name: Low-level laser therapy / photobiomodulation
oneLiner: Home ear-lasers are sold online today; the meta-analysis verdict is null — and statistically unlikely to change.
whatItIs: Red/near-infrared laser applied to the ear or mastoid, claimed to boost cochlear cell function. Sold as home devices (TinniTool, TINNImed and generic 'red light therapy' products, ~$300–500).
howItWorks: Photobiomodulation can affect mitochondrial function in tissue; there is no validated pathway to reducing chronic tinnitus.

loudness.summary: 2020 systematic review with meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis: no significant benefit — and TSA indicates more identical trials are unlikely to change that.

regulatory.detail: CE marking of a low-risk device is not evidence of efficacy.

safety: Low physical risk at consumer powers; financial risk is the issue.

bestResult: Isolated small positive trials, not replicated in aggregate
limitations: Meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis is null

name: Cannabis / CBD
oneLiner: 'CBD for tinnitus' is aggressively marketed. There are zero human trials — and population data point the wrong way.
whatItIs: Cannabis and cannabidiol products marketed for tinnitus relief, riding the general CBD wellness wave (~20% of US adults used CBD in 2022).
howItWorks: Cannabinoid receptors exist in auditory pathways, but animal models suggest cannabinoids may INDUCE or worsen tinnitus-like activity, not reduce it.
mechanism: None validated; preclinical signal points toward harm

loudness.summary: No human trials at all.

distress.summary: No human trials. NHANES population analysis: tinnitus prevalence is HIGHER among cannabis users (OR ~1.8 for high-volume use, adjusted).

regulatory.detail: No product has any tinnitus authorization anywhere.

safety: Drug interactions, dependence potential (THC), unregulated product quality — plus the epidemiological association with more tinnitus, not less.
bestSuitedFor: Nobody, for tinnitus
bestResult: None — no trials exist
limitations: Zero human trials
